full_judgment:
2. The complaint case assumed existence out of a petition filed by one Md Gyesuddin, a resident of Chittagong. In his petition the complainant alleged that being desirous to buy a parcel of land, he approached the appellant to obtain latter's opinion of the title of the said property. After examining relevant Khatians, etc., the appellant, gave a clean bill as to the apparent vendor's title and possession over the property in question. He also expressed that the property was free of encumbrances. The appellant, instead of returning the Original Khatian, handed back the photocopies thereof to the complainant. Being stimulated by the said affirmative opinion, the complainant entered into a bainanama in respect to the said land, which venture taxed his pocket by an amount in excess of Taka 5,00,000 in all. At a subsequent stage the complainant got swamped with suspicion about the authenticity of the photocopies of the said documents, which state of his mind propelled him to procure certified copies of the same. Said copies revealed that the subject property was indeed part of government's khas land. He further alleged that the spurious opinion furnished by the opposite party was the outcome of an intrigue espoused by the appellant in connivance with the fake vendor. 

 7. Tribunal No. 2 of the Bar Council after recording evidence and reckoning sub-missions, passed the Order under appeal stating, "On a careful examination of written statement, deposition of opposite party Advocate and other connected papers submitted to this Tribunal, it appears to us that on the basis of the advice of the opposite party Advocate and on the basis of the bainapatra, the complainant made a deal to purchase with Hari Ranjan and paid him the earnest money of Taka 61,050 and also spent some money by way of development of the contracted land. Had the learned opposite party Advocate advised the complainant properly and correctly, he would not get involved in the deal incurring financial loss. The loss incurred to the complainant is due to unprofessional and dubious role of the Advocate. As an Advocate he ought to have been more cautious to preserve the interest of his client. It appears to the Tribunal that the opposite party Advocate in order to make some gain had drafted and written the bainapatra without caring to examine as to whether the seller had title over the land or not. It is clear that the landed properties contracted is a khas land of the government which could have attracted the notice of a man with ordinary prudence but the learned Advocate had collusively without caring to see to the interest of his client thought of his fees only and drafted the bainapatra which caused loss to complainant."
